title: Fragmentation patterns
keyIdea: In a mass spectrometer, the molecular ion M⁺• can break apart. One bond splits, giving a positive fragment ion and a neutral radical: M⁺• → X⁺ + Y•. Only the ion is deflected and detected, so each fragment peak has the m/z of a cation. Common fragments are CH₃⁺ (15), C₂H₅⁺ (29), CH₃CO⁺ or C₃H₇⁺ (43), CH₂OH⁺ (31) and C₆H₅⁺ (77). The tallest (base) peak comes from the most stable cation, such as an acylium ion RCO⁺ or a secondary carbocation. Isomers share M⁺ but break differently, so their fragments tell them apart: propan-1-ol gives 31, propan-2-ol gives 45.
familyTip: Take any small molecule, such as butanone, and draw its structure. Break each bond in turn and write both possible cations with their masses (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16). Then look up its real spectrum (the NIST Chemistry WebBook is free) and tick off which fragments appear.

visual.caption: Which molecule makes each fragment peak? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: snip bonds in butanone to make fragment peaks, put the charge on the detected piece, predict base peaks, tell isomers apart and label a spectrum.

kid: The molecular ion M⁺• has lost one electron. It has a + charge and one odd electron. It has spare energy, so it often breaks. One bond splits into two pieces.

One piece keeps the charge. It is a cation, X⁺. The other piece gets the odd electron. It is a neutral radical, Y•. Only ions are bent by the field and reach the detector. So one break gives one peak, at the mass of the cation.
Learn the common peaks. CH₃⁺ is 15. C₂H₅⁺ is 29. CH₃CO⁺ is 43, and so is C₃H₇⁺. CH₂OH⁺ is 31. C₆H₅⁺ is 77. Work out others with C = 12, H = 1 and O = 16.

The tallest peak is the base peak. It comes from the most stable cation, since more of those form. RCO⁺ ions and cations with more groups on the charged carbon are stable. Isomers have the same M⁺. Their fragments differ, so use them to tell the isomers apart.
adult: Ages 17 to 18, A-level Chemistry (organic analysis by mass spectrometry). Students explain that the molecular ion breaks into a cation and a radical. They write an equation for a fragmentation, link major peaks to fragments and use fragments to tell isomers apart, such as propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.

In electron impact, M loses an electron to give M⁺•, a radical cation. One bond breaks to give X⁺ + Y•, or X• + Y⁺. Only the cation is detected. For a 1+ ion, its m/z is its mass. Peak height depends on how stable the cation is. Acylium ions RCO⁺ give the base peak: 43 in propanone and butanone, 57 in pentan-3-one. CH₂OH⁺ (31) is the base peak of propan-1-ol, and CH₃CHOH⁺ (45) of propan-2-ol.

Common mistakes: drawing both pieces as ions or both as radicals; putting the + on the piece whose mass does not match the peak; taking the base peak to be M⁺, which is often small; and naming isomers from M⁺ alone. Careful: 43 can be CH₃CO⁺ or C₃H₇⁺, and 29 can be C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺, so check which one the structure can make.

In the lab the learner breaks bonds in butanone and chooses which piece keeps the charge until four peaks appear, then drags the + to the detected piece in four equations. They predict three base peaks, match five spectra to one of two isomers and label five peaks of butanone.

practice.prompt: In M⁺• → X⁺ + Y•, which species is detected?
practice.hint: Only charged particles are deflected and reach the detector.
practice.explain: X⁺ is a cation, so it is detected. Y• is a neutral radical, so it is not.

practice.prompt: An alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = {n} loses CH₃•. At what m/z is the fragment peak?
practice.hint: Mr of CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is 12n + (2n + 2). Then take away 15 for CH₃.
practice.explain: Mr = 14 × {n} + 2 = {=14*n+2}. Losing CH₃ (15) leaves a cation at m/z {=14*n+2-15}.

practice.prompt: A ketone shows its base peak at m/z 43. Which fragment is it most likely to be?
practice.hint: Work out 12 + 3 + 12 + 16, and think about which ions are stable.
practice.explain: CH₃CO⁺ = 12 + 3 + 12 + 16 = 43, a stable acylium ion. C₂H₅⁺ is 29 and CH₃⁺ is 15.

practice.prompt: A molecular ion with M = {m} loses C₂H₅•. At what m/z is the fragment peak?
practice.explain: C₂H₅ = 29, so the cation is at {m} − 29 = {=m-29}.

practice.prompt: Which peak tells propan-1-ol apart from propan-2-ol?
practice.hint: The two have the same Mr, so look at the fragments.
practice.explain: Propan-1-ol makes CH₂OH⁺ (31); propan-2-ol makes CH₃CHOH⁺ (45). Both have M⁺ at 60.

pool.prompt: Which equation shows a fragmentation correctly?
pool.hint: One piece keeps the charge; the other takes the odd electron.
pool.explain: The charge stays on one piece and the odd electron goes to the other: CH₃CO⁺ + CH₃•.

pool.prompt: An aromatic compound has a peak at m/z 77. Which ion is it?
pool.explain: C₆H₅⁺ = 72 + 5 = 77. C₆H₆ is 78, and a radical is not detected.

pool.prompt: Why is the peak at m/z 43 taller than M⁺ (58) in propanone?
choices: CH₃CO⁺ is a stable cation, and many M⁺ ions break up to form it
CH₃⁺ is the most stable ion
pool.hint: Peak height reflects how many of that ion reach the detector.
pool.explain: Many M⁺• ions fragment before detection, and the stable acylium ion CH₃CO⁺ forms readily, so 43 is the base peak.

pool.prompt: A ketone CH₃CO–R has M = {m}. It splits into CH₃CO⁺ and R•. What is the mass of R?
pool.hint: CH₃CO has mass 43; the rest of the molecule is R.
pool.explain: R = {m} − 43 = {=m-43}. The peak itself is at 43, because only CH₃CO⁺ is detected.

pool.prompt: Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one both have M⁺ at 86. Which spectrum is pentan-3-one?
pool.hint: Pentan-3-one is C₂H₅COC₂H₅. Which acylium ion can it make?
pool.explain: Pentan-3-one gives C₂H₅CO⁺ at 57. Pentan-2-one has a CH₃ next to the C=O, so it gives CH₃CO⁺ at 43.

pool.prompt: A peak at m/z 29 in an aldehyde could be which two ions?
pool.explain: CHO⁺ = 29 and C₂H₅⁺ = 29. CH₃CO⁺ and C₃H₇⁺ are both 43.

pool.prompt: An alcohol CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH with n = {n} loses a CH₃• radical. At what m/z is the fragment peak?
pool.hint: Mr of CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH is 14n + 18. Take away 15 for CH₃.
pool.explain: Mr = 14 × {n} + 18 = {=14*n+18}. Losing CH₃ (15) gives a peak at {=14*n+18-15}.

pool.prompt: A student says the base peak is always the molecular ion. What is wrong?
choices: M⁺ is often small; the base peak is the most stable fragment
the base peak is always at m/z 15
the base peak is the lightest ion
pool.hint: Think about what happens to most M⁺• ions before they reach the detector.
pool.explain: Many molecular ions break up, so M⁺ is often small. The base peak is the most abundant ion, usually a stable fragment.
